issue.title: [Hero Run] 535B-A23B on 18T tokens
issue.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

issue.title: [grug] Ragged EP train step hangs silently on one rack at d6144 hero scale
issue.body:
The ragged all-to-all EP backend hangs at the d6144 hero scale (11 racks, 704 GPUs) within the first hundred steps, on both attempts of the 2026-09-02 deployment. The train step never completes on one rack, the other ten spin in the next AllReduce, and levanter's progress watchdog kills the gang 15 minutes later (`No progress after train_step_started for 909.8 seconds (timeout 900.0); terminating with exit code 124`). No rank logs an error: nothing from NCCL, XLA, CUDA (no Xid), the allocator, or Kubernetes. The hero was rolled back to `04751985c7` (pooled-wave backend), which resumed cleanly from the same checkpoint.

Deployment: main `8e48cdb3ca`, run `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k` resuming `hero-12d8b6f0-dee637` from its `step-54000` permanent checkpoint (#8868), `HERO_WATCH_INTERVAL = 10`, `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true --xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall`, jax 0.11.1, NCCL 2.30.7. Coordinator `/marin/hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k-coord-aade2815`; both attempts ran on the same 176 nodes.

- Attempt 0: steps 54001–54070 completed normally (loss tracks the pooled-wave run step for step at −0.006 nats, drops 3.4e-2 → <1e-4, MFU 20.5 → 23.4%, peak HBM 103.6 GiB). Step 54071 started at 00:23:30Z and never finished; killed 00:38:46Z.
- Attempt 1: restored the same checkpoint, completed step 54000 at 00:45:38Z (loss 1.2364, identical to attempt 0), then hung on step 54001; killed ~01:01Z.

Both hangs are on the first plain train step after a `diagnostic_watch_step` step (54070 → 54071 after seven clean alternations; 54000 → 54001 on the first). The plain and watch steps are two XLA executables that share the NCCL symmetric-memory arena for the ragged all-to-all: each registers its own window at the arena base (`AcquireSymmetricMemory`, `CollectiveMemoryCache`), and equal footprints coexist. #8861 is the same design failing the other way: an executable with a *different* footprint (the capacity-limited eval) makes the next train step fail with `ncclGroupEnd() failed: invalid argument`. Here the footprints are equal and the failure is a silent hang instead of an error, so #8859 (dropless eval only) removes the crash but not this.

Evidence that the hang sits on one rack's EP domain rather than a node fault:

- NCCL RAS (periodic `STATUS` from process 0, `telemetry_v1.levanter`): six minutes into each hang, 64 cross-rack communicators show an AllReduce operation-count skew of exactly 3 (attempt 0: min 10509 / max 10512 at 00:29:43Z; attempt 1: 190 / 193 at 00:52:30Z) and the 704-rank communicator a skew of 2. Before the hangs every communicator was in sync. One member per cross-rack communicator behind by the same count is one whole rack that never entered the step's trailing AllReduces.
- Iris per-task CPU (`iris.task`): exactly 16 of 176 tasks ran at ~4.0 cores while the other 160 ran at ~8.0 during each hang, i.e. one rack in a different wait state from the ranks busy-polling in AllReduce. Attempt 0: tasks 128–143 (zone 129, nodes `s38vxs64 s45sxs64 s51vxs64 s5xvxs64 s69vxs64 s7htxs64 s7qvxs64 s8ktxs64 s8mtxs64 s8yvxs64 s9jvxs64 s9lrxs64 scspxs64 scssxs64 sd8sxs64 shmsxs64`). Attempt 1: tasks 64–79, a different rack on the same node set.
- py-spy thread dumps (`iris process profile threads`) of tasks 0, 83, and 140 during attempt 0: every rank's main thread inside `train_step` (`train.py:1176`), no Python-side wait; the hang is below XLA's dispatch.
- No node conditions or events on either rack; the cluster's six `HPCVerification=Fail` nodes are elsewhere.

The stall-triggered verbose RAS capture (`trigger = stall`) published nothing in either attempt, so the rank-level view that would name the stuck ranks and the pending collective is missing; the periodic sample is all we have. Neither a 200-step 1-rack smoke restoring the same checkpoint (20 watch/plain alternations) nor the 11,420-step d768 rung reproduced it, so the failure needs more than one rack, i.e. more than one EP domain sharing the job.

Side observations from the same deployment: a cold compile at this shape took 22.9 min for the watch executable plus 6.6 min for the plain one; the data loader's second 64-item prefetch took 920 s (overlapped by compile) where the pooled-wave hero's restarts took under 100 s.

Done when: the ragged backend runs at 11 racks through at least several hundred steps with watch steps enabled without a hang, or the hang is reproduced at smaller multi-rack scale with a GPU-side stack (CUDA core dump / `cuda-gdb` on a stuck rank) that names the kernel or collective.

Related: #8861 (symmetric-window overlap between executables), #8859, #8868, #8506 (hero status log). Side-by-side trial report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/ep_change:-hero-ragged-a2a-swap,-200-step-trial--VmlldzoxNzg1ODIzMA==

issue.title: [epic][sft] Establish a versioned cold-start SFT recipe
issue.body:
Establish a versioned cold-start SFT recipe that runs immediately after pretraining cool-down. The recipe should produce a model with the core capabilities needed by Marin's post-training and evaluation workflows.

The initial competency set is:

- Chat-template adherence and basic instruction following.
- Think blocks.
- Thinking across science, mathematics, legal, and medical contexts.
- Adaptive thinking effort.
- Model-name responses.
- Basic agentic tool use.
- Answer-format hardening.
- Task summarization.
- Resuming a task from a summary.

Related preceding work: #7321 and #7743.

Research issues:

- #8093: adaptive thinking effort.
- #8094: model-name response behavior.
- #8092: answer-format hardening.
- #8095: task summarization.
- #8091: resume tasks from summaries.
- #8090: cross-domain thinking and basic agentic tool use.

Done when:

- A recipe version identifies its parent checkpoint, tokenizer and chat template, data mixture and immutable revisions, training configuration, and export contract.
- The recipe has acceptance evaluations for every listed competency, with recorded baseline comparisons and failure criteria.
- The recipe can be run after a pretraining cool-down without experiment-specific manual wiring.
- The selected recipe and its evidence are documented in the repository.

issue.title: [inference] Hero vLLM decode throughput on GB200: tracking
issue.body:
## TL;DR

Hero (Mochi, 535B-A23B MoE) BF16 vLLM decode on GB200 is step-latency bound. Per-step time stays at 56–78 ms from 1 to 128 sequences per DP engine, so output throughput rises almost linearly with batch size until `max_num_seqs` caps it. Raising `max_num_seqs` from 32 to 64 doubles throughput at 1,024 concurrent requests (+95% to +99% in three same-node pairs, about 500 → 1,000 output tokens/s/GPU). Correctness gates pass, and latency at lower concurrency is unchanged. `max_num_seqs` 128 reached 3.6–3.8× the baseline cap at 2,048 concurrent requests (1,839 output tokens/s/GPU on a fast node set). `max_num_seqs` 256 gains nothing more, because the KV cache fills at about 250 sequences of 1K tokens per engine. With 4K outputs the KV cache fills at about 100–128 sequences per engine: 96 per engine (1,536 in flight) gives about 1,540 output tokens/s/GPU without waiting, and 128 gives 1,785–1,850 while KV-bound (R11). The `0ac9dcb` wheel from #11241 is throughput-neutral against `3004cd8` and is the current baseline. TP2 from vllm#119, a 2,048 → 8,192 prefill budget, and the one-sided NVLink all-to-all did not improve this workload. Most of the decode step is host overhead from the eager ShortConv op between piecewise graphs; letting decode replay full CUDA graphs (a two-line fork guard relaxation, R12) cuts the step 2.0–3.8× and raises throughput 43% at 1,024 in flight, with all gates passing (an apparent long-prompt slowdown did not reproduce). On top of that, a tuned GB200 fused-MoE config (+7%, R14) and NCCL symmetric memory for the MoE collectives (+6%, R15) each add throughput at 1,024 in flight, and four API servers lift 2,048 in flight by 13% (R13), where one API server had become the limit. Stacked in an A/B/A run on a fast node set (R16), the full set reaches about 1,430 output tokens/s/GPU at 1,024 in flight and 2,390 at 2,048, against about 1,050 and 1,840 for the best PIECEWISE configuration (cross-run), at 18.6 ms/token for a single request.

## Description

The objective is output tokens/s per GPU under RL-rollout-like load, with time to first token (TTFT) and inter-token latency (ITL) as guardrails. Precision stays BF16; FP8 is out of scope for now.

Setup for every measurement below:

- Weights: the SFT checkpoint `step-400407` exported as BF16 safetensors (export schema 3), `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/exports/mochi-sft/hero-sft-fullab-step393k-v2/step-400407/2af3f828aa-cpu-a1` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fexports%2Fmochi-sft%2Fhero-sft-fullab-step393k-v2%2Fstep-400407%2F2af3f828aa-cpu-a1)). Router and experts are stored in placed order `1e80fa529585`.
- Serving: Marin vLLM fork release `marin-vllm-gpu-20261113-0ac9dcb157ee`, the #11241 pin (`3004cd8f1632` before it was accepted).
- Topology: one 4-node GB200 gang (16 GPUs) in one NVLink domain on cw-us-east-08a, TP1 / DP16 / EP16, all-to-all `allgather_reducescatter`, Triton MoE, FlashInfer attention.
- Batching and context: `max_num_seqs` 32, `max_num_batched_tokens` 2,048, prefix caching off, `max_model_len` 262,144, one API server.
- Compilation: PIECEWISE CUDA graphs with `splitting_ops` = `unified_attention_with_output`, `unified_kv_cache_update`, `grug_moe_short_conv`.

This is the same configuration as the team's BF16 serving endpoint for the checkpoint (`hero-sft-step400407-bf16`). Its batch-1 decode reproduces that endpoint's logged ITL: 56 ms here against 58 ms.

Load: 1,024 GSM8K test questions with the Marin chat template (mean prompt 70 tokens), temperature 1.0, a fixed seed per request, `ignore_eos`, 1,024 output tokens per request. The loop is closed: the generator keeps a fixed number of requests in flight, three waves per point. Throughput is the output-token rate from when all in-flight requests have produced their first token until the last submission, divided by 16 GPUs. A batch-1 point (8 × 256 tokens) gives single-request latency.

Each candidate runs on the same 4 nodes as its control, back to back in one job. GB200 node sets on the cluster differ by about 20% in throughput for identical software, so unpaired comparisons are not used.

## Correctness gates (v4)

The JAX reference is Levanter scoring the same `step-400407` checkpoint in placed order: BF16 weights, fp32 log-softmax, zero dropped MoE assignments, and a router bias that matches the export to 2.4e-7. It covers 11,370 positions in 32 fixed histories (GSM8K chat prompts and book excerpts, 40–1,835 tokens), plus 4K, 32K and 65K book histories (last 512 positions and every 256th). Outputs: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/reference/ref-a4/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Freference%2Fref-a4%2F)).

- (a) Hard: prompt scoring on DP engine 0 is bitwise identical across three passes within one server instance: alone, while the other 15 engines decode 8 requests each, and alone again.
- (b) Hard: the per-position maximum probability error of vLLM's top-5 against the JAX top-64 stays inside the control band for p50, p90, p99 and the fraction above 0.075, on both the short histories and the long histories. The band is the union of per-run 95% bootstrap intervals (whole histories resampled) over 5 control runs. Band, short histories: p90 [0.018, 0.034], p99 [0.066, 0.114], fraction above 0.075 [0.7%, 2.5%]. Band, long histories: p90 [0.022, 0.026], p99 [0.049, 0.069].
- (c) Decode non-regression against the control, distributional.
- (d) The decode load-dependence defect below is measured for every candidate. A change in it is called only after repeats.
- (e) From R12 on: decode self-consistency. The 32 gate histories are greedy-decoded for 256 tokens, alone on engine 0 and then 32 per engine on all 16 engines at once. Each prompt plus continuation is then scored by prefill on the same engine. The per-token difference |p_decode − p_prefill| of the chosen token (p50, p90, p99, maximum, fraction above 0.075) must stay at the control's level on the same nodes. Gate (b) covers prefill only; (e) covers the decode path, which can execute differently (for example, in full CUDA graphs).
- CUDA graphs must be captured; a run aborts if vLLM resolves `cudagraph_mode` to NONE.

An absolute 0.075 maximum is not used. At 11,370 positions the control itself reaches 0.50 at near-tie positions. Cross-run bitwise equality is also not used: fresh compiles of an unchanged config differ (see below).

## Results

"In flight" is the number of requests the server is processing at once (the closed-loop concurrency of the load generator, across all 16 GPUs). It is not a context length. Every row uses the same sequences of about 1,100 tokens (a 70-token prompt plus 1,024 sampled output tokens), except R10 and R11, which generate 4,096 output tokens. Throughput is output tokens/s per GPU. Each candidate ran back to back with its control on the same 4 nodes.

Decision rule: a candidate is decided on output tokens/s per GPU at 1,024 requests in flight (2,048 for the `max_num_seqs` 64 → 128 step and for the KV-bound 4K rows; 512 for rows that were swept only to 512). A change counts as a gain only beyond ±2%, the spread measured between same-node pairs that should be equal (the wheel pairs and the `max_num_seqs` pairs at 512 in flight). Latency columns are guardrails. Verdict words: "gain accepted" improves the deciding metric; "adopted, neutral" was taken for another reason with no measurable throughput effect; "no effect"; "rejected".

R0 is the mean of the `max_num_seqs` 32 controls measured on fast node sets, with the range and run count. No `max_num_seqs` 32 control was measured at 2,048 in flight on a fast node set, so that cell is blank.

## Known defects

- Open: decode is not invariant to load on other DP engines. Engine 0 decodes the same prompts alone, then while the other 15 engines are busy. Only 1–2% of its decode steps keep a bitwise-identical top-1 log-probability. Top-1 |Δp| reaches p90 0.013–0.016 and max 0.09–0.11 (0.16–0.20 nats); greedy tokens flip, once at a 0.43-nat margin. Load on engine 0 itself gives the same size of change. Repeated runs alone are bitwise identical, and prompt scoring (prefill) under peer load is bitwise identical. Both wheels show it. Mechanism measured (R18): DP padding runs every engine at the largest token count of any engine, so peer load moves engine 0 to a larger CUDA graph size; engine 0 stays bitwise unchanged while peers do not raise its padded size. A single capture size (`cudagraph_capture_sizes` = [`max_num_seqs`]) makes decode bitwise invariant to peer load, at a latency cost when engines are not full; dependence on engine 0's own batch remains, smaller.
- Fresh compiles of an unchanged config produce different numerics. Five compiles of `3004cd8` fell into three groups. Within a group, scoring is bitwise identical. Between groups, scoring differs at 99.5% of positions (|Δp| p99 0.072–0.075, max 0.48–0.56). The distributional statistics against JAX barely move: short-history p90 0.0270–0.0273, p99 0.0871–0.0885. Kernel autotuning or benchmarking at compile time is the suspected cause. Disabling Inductor's combo-kernel benchmarking did not remove the modes (R8), so the cause is still open.
- A Hero launch whose `--compilation-config` omits `vllm::grug_moe_short_conv` from `splitting_ops` runs without CUDA graphs. The fork's ShortConv guard sets `cudagraph_mode` to NONE with only a log line. Batch-1 decode was 182 ms/token against 56 ms with graphs.
- Open: three Triton kernels compile during serving instead of at startup (seen in the baseline and `0ac9dcb` server logs): `_causal_conv`, `fused_moe_kernel` and `_topk_log_softmax_kernel`. Inferred, not measured: the first requests that reach them pay the compile time. Fixed on a local fork branch (R28): no compile after startup, gates pass, no throughput change; a fork PR is drafted.
- Two GB200 node sets ran about 18–25% slower for both wheels: s76txs64, s9jtxs64, s7xsxs64, s8ltxs64 (rack 125) and s7psxs64, s96txs64, sbftxs64, sb3txs64 (rack 124). The cause is undetermined. With full CUDA graphs (R12) the gap disappears: single-request decode is 20.2–20.4 ms/token on a slow rack-122 set, a rack-125 set and a fast rack-394 set; the penalty is in the host-bound part of the PIECEWISE step (inferred).
- vllm#119 at `ef7f5a0` (the TP2/TP6 numbers in #11320) predates vllm#121, the position-dependent query scaling that export schema 3 requires. A merge onto `0ac9dcb` needed three fixes: allow Hero TP for schema 3, apply the TP2 NCCL guard to schema 3, and reshape Q by the per-rank head count in log scaling. Without the last, TP>1 crashes.

## Open questions

- The KV cache, not per-step time, caps the batch (R7): about 220 sequences per engine at 1K tokens and about 97 at 4K, from the fork's block accounting (4 attention groups at 16 tokens per block, with sliding-window groups holding every token below 2,048, plus 12 ShortConv state blocks). Fork changes could add about 12.5% (store 6 global KV heads instead of 12) and about 3% (ShortConv page padding). The 4K-output runs (R10, R11) matched the model: KV use was 31.7% at 32 sequences per engine and 47.2% at 48, and the cache filled with 96–128 sequences running per engine.
- The load generator stays below one core up to 4,096 requests in flight; four API servers lower TTFT but not throughput (R4b).
- Long-context parity is measured through 262K (R25): against two context-parallel JAX references, vLLM's scoring at 131K and 262K, including the log-scaled region past 65,536, agrees as well as at 65K.
- Throughput on long-context agentic traffic, where TP2 may help (#11320).

## Links

- #10388 Hero RL readiness on H100 and GB200
- #11127 Export, serve and RL-train the log-scaled hero
- #11241 vLLM `0ac9dcb` adoption
- #11320 AgentX and vLLM throughput tuning guide
- marin-community/vllm#119 Hero tensor parallelism
- marin-community/vllm#121 Hero global-layer query scaling by position

issue.title: [rl] Add the 262K three-rack Mochi example
issue.body:
Add `--profile three-rack` to the Mochi launcher in #11321. It uses a 262,144-token context, 64 trainer GPUs at TP1/PP16/CP4/EP4 and eight 16-GPU inference engines at TP1/PP1/DP16/EP16. Required NVLink placement puts the trainer in one domain and four engines in each of two further domains: 48 four-GPU hosts in total.

Inference uses FlashInfer, PIECEWISE graphs and the published BF16 vLLM build, with verified expert-block weight publication. Normal admission permits up to 128 prompt groups, bounded by batch size and staleness. Both profiles retain the Mochi adaptation of Ben’s workflow: 32 groups of eight samples, staleness three, equal SWE/nonagentic quotas, Hero MuonH, held-out evaluation and native checkpoints every two updates, and a ten-hour RL budget. Best selection needs 120 scores and five complete evaluations. The one-rack configuration is unchanged.

The [recipe](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/goal/mochi-three-rack-review-01a1c926/docs/recipes/mochi-rl.md) gives fresh, native-continuation and explicit `--smoke` commands using retained model/data handles. Smoke keeps its two-group admission cap. Use a new output version when switching from the earlier two-engine EP64 layout. Preserve same-version recovery for that new run. The trainer retains activation fusion, pinned checkpoint inputs, 256-KiB communication buffers and InfiniBand.

A matched 64-GPU serving comparison rose from 126 to 464 output tokens/s per allocated inference GPU, a 3.68x serving gain across several settings. It does not measure RL speedup. The new inference settings completed three fresh RL updates at a 102,400-token context limit, with a first-batch maximum of 56,196 attended tokens, verified publication and later generation in all eight engines, two fully scored 120-task evaluations and a native checkpoint. That run used separate task-setup/runtime repairs and cadence. Two evaluations do not complete the five-evaluation selection window. Integrated near-262K training, sustained completion and live same-version recovery remain unqualified.

The independent configuration guide for main is in #11609. Keep this runnable example draft and unmerged while the Long and Quick Loops converge. It remains based on `stack/mochi-ben-one-rack-01a1d2a9` at `75bf9fba6c8419070e87c9f97ddd0478148a27a9`, over fixed runtime integration [89c1de503cdb](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/89c1de503cdbdbd97eaa7a5349970fe4806c1b5e). No dependency refresh is included. CPU checks cover normal/smoke, fresh/resume, response and batch overrides, native placement and unchanged one-rack configurations.

issue.title: [rl] 64 MiB MIN/MAX reductions corrupt 32-rank replica verification
issue.body:
Large NCCL MIN/MAX reductions return incorrect values in the initialized SkyRL policy runtime and make strict replica verification reject matching weights.

Reproduce:
1. Initialize the production Ray policy workers on 64 GB200s in one NVLink domain, with PP2/CP4/EP4/DP8, NCCL 2.30.7 and `NCCL_BUFFSIZE=262144`. Retain the actual Megatron data-parallel groups including context parallelism: 32 ranks per pipeline stage.
2. Inside each worker, run this known-input check on its existing group before weight publication:

Pinned inputs: diagnostic revision `767592680758e3bc47c5ecda385973c3199ca033`, frozen configuration SHA256 `0d4ca250683aaa64d295c4137677709b00941ad8ff307055afdf7e5b63e5a2ce`, and the same adopted Snowball SFT export (input artifact version `2026.11.17.1`, identity suffix `81b4d4d5`). Task image: `ghcr.io/marin-community/iris-task@sha256:13519c59442bd70ed5ec2902869f15094992d6849d7e34e353f1338dec7ff5f8`, frozen `megatron production` bootstrap. The Linux runtime manifest pins PyTorch 2.14.1; the loaded PyTorch version was not independently captured in these receipts.

```python
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import megatron.core.parallel_state as mpu

group = mpu.get_data_parallel_group(with_context_parallel=True)
members = dist.get_process_group_ranks(group)
base = torch.arange(16_777_216, device="cuda", dtype=torch.int32) % 128
source = base + dist.get_rank()
low, high = source.clone(), source.clone()
dist.all_reduce(low, op=dist.ReduceOp.MIN, group=group)
dist.all_reduce(high, op=dist.ReduceOp.MAX, group=group)
assert torch.equal(low, base + min(members))
assert torch.equal(high, base + max(members))
```

Expected: exact integer MIN/MAX values on every member, with source bytes unchanged.

Observed: all 64 workers fail on 64 MiB arrays in their two 32-rank dense groups. Rank 0 has 11,620,913 wrong MIN elements and 11,652,720 wrong MAX elements. The same handles pass at 1,024 and 4,194,305 elements. The eight-rank expert groups pass all three sizes. Independent NumPy hashes confirm the results; all 128 failed output hashes differ from every possible rank-offset reference pattern, which excludes a simple wrong-member set as the explanation.

At the strict comparator boundary, all 117,568 live sender tensors retain their entry/exit hashes, data/storage pointers, offsets, strides and tensor IDs. Actual group names and members match the expected geometry. Replica hashes agree, source intervals do not overlap, and input bytes stay unchanged during the known-input reductions. The unchanged `compare_replicas` then reports 876,550,056–945,509,596 mismatched bytes per rank. Its current 16 MiB raw-byte chunks create 64 MiB int32 reduction buffers: [comparison code on main](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3e8c7baa26a451b1f8c630bd6dc68a7135907a32/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/weight_sync/expert_block/verify_weights.py#L91).

A separate eight-GPU control passes Ray/torchrun, masked/unmasked GPU visibility and `NCCL_BUFFSIZE` unset/262144. This report therefore reproduces the defect inside the initialized 64-worker runtime; an equivalent standalone 32-worker reproduction and the exact NCCL/PyTorch mechanism remain unproven.

Proposed mitigation, not implemented or GPU-qualified: bound raw-byte comparison chunks to 4 MiB so each int32 reduction is 16 MiB, while comparing every byte with the same strict MIN/MAX rule. Keep the failing 64 MiB case as a correctness regression and investigate the runtime cause separately.

Pinned analysis and all 516 raw-receipt SHA256 values: `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/experiments/nccl-minmax-32-rank-20261118/analysis-v1.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fexperiments%2Fnccl-minmax-32-rank-20261118%2Fanalysis-v1.json)). Diagnostic source revision: `767592680758e3bc47c5ecda385973c3199ca033` (local research commit, not yet published). No fix commit or further GPU iteration has been made.

issue.title: [long-loop] First expert-MuonH train step stalls on 64 H100s
issue.body:
## Summary

On the 64-H100 Long Loop layout with XLA autotune level 0, EAGER CUDA module loading has not eliminated the intermittent first-step stall. On source `5cbfba9f`, both fresh-state expert-MuonH runs without a host rebind (G5 and G20) stalled on their first stock call; they were submitted 60 ms apart and shared fabric. In the recorded EAGER/autotune-0 BF16 cohort with host rebind, six first stock calls completed (v9, C-replay r3, C-e12, G5r2, G20r2 and G0r2) and one stalled (G0). These observations do not isolate a rebind effect or estimate failure rates.

Three C150 base-start treatment arms, with routed experts on Adam, each completed 150 updates with EAGER and no rebind. The plain control is outside that count. This is a different optimizer path and does not establish that EAGER fixes the expert-MuonH stall. The runtime mechanism remains unknown. See [the draft launch change](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11647).

## Distinct observations

- **First-step stall:** G5 and G20 stalled with EAGER and no rebind on the `5cbfba9f` expert-MuonH path. G0 also stalled after its host rebind, with EAGER and autotune level 0.
- **NCCL initialization:** In a task-0 capture, five G20-FP32 r2 worker main threads were waiting in `NcclCollectives::CreateCommunicatorsWithCancel` during clique initialization. A matching relaunch completed. This is a separate observed signature; its cause and any connection to the first-step stall remain unresolved.
- **Slow steps:** Earlier BF16 runs showed approximately 115–132 seconds per step, and G5-FP32 showed approximately 120–134 seconds per step after step 1. Faster observations were approximately 39–52 seconds per step. Whether these observations share a cause is unknown.

## Earlier observations

Earlier LAZY runs stalled or ran slowly. An earlier EAGER/autotune-0 fresh-state H run without a host round trip completed its first two stock calls in 58.2 and 49.1 seconds and logged a first loss of 0.6393635273. Carried-state v9, C-replay r3 and C-e12 also completed their first EAGER/autotune-0 stock calls. An older EAGER run with autotune level 4 on a different graph stalled in `cuModuleLoadData`.

## Symptom

The Long Loop Grug MoE SFT loop can stall in its first compiled train step on eight hosts with eight H100s each. All 64 GPUs stayed busy, but the step did not complete. Among the Long Loop runs examined, the stall has been observed only in graphs with expert weights in MuonH. The stalled loop is on the Long Loop branch, not main. A related first-update stall on a different layout is tracked in [the Snowball optimizer issue](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11440); a common cause is not established.

## Observed setup and expected behavior

Run the Long Loop SFT graph from commit `917055e33f44ddb3b5e1a927eab0793e7a9f4501` with replica=1, data=8, expert=1 and context=8 across eight H100 hosts, with expert matrices in MuonH. The first train step should finish and subsequent steps should run without a host round trip. Two runs stalled before completing that step.

A successful diagnostic retained the compiled executable reference while it snapshotted the entire train state to host memory, deleted its device arrays, and restored the state before the first call. Its first three steps took 80.7, 49.0 and 41.1 seconds. In a separate paired diagnostic, a direct compiled call and the subsequent stock call took 52.5 and 46.1 seconds; the latter followed a direct execution and a host state reconstruction.

## Evidence and limits

Isolated expert momentum, projection and Newton–Schulz probes completed. In the paired diagnostic, StableHLO and optimized HLO were byte-identical and all 76 input leaf metadata entries matched; the stock call made no rank-zero compiler requests. Disabling the persistent executable cache did not prevent the stall, and the successful reconstruction run used autotune level zero. Its pre-reconstruction buffer inventory found no shared buffer start addresses and no pending shards on all 64 ranks. The cancelled stalled attempts did not retain those buffer inventories, so this does not establish their buffer state.

The cause is unknown. Whether the same mechanism also explains the observed slow steps remains open. The highest observed per-task sample was 146.2 GiB against a 640 GiB allocation. The snapshot peak was not measured.

The v7a2 rank-zero runtime inventory reports JAX, jaxlib, jax-cuda13-plugin and jax-cuda13-pjrt 0.11.1 and CUDA runtime 13.0.96. The source declares `jax[cuda13]==0.11.0` in its root dependency set; the installed rank-zero inventory is the runtime observation. All eight task image pull events identify `ghcr.io/marin-community/iris-task@sha256:b5b474d80ca79f996049cc0cf700ab93ab2d41a4d9b8a91afc43ce11bf44d974`.

Evidence is stored in 02a temporary prefixes and expires after 30 days:

- Reconstruction run: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/e12/h-muon-prelude-v7a2-20261118/fresh/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fe12%2Fh-muon-prelude-v7a2-20261118%2Ffresh%2F)).
- Paired HLO evidence: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/e12/h-muon-dispatch-v6-20261118/fresh/evidence/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fe12%2Fh-muon-dispatch-v6-20261118%2Ffresh%2Fevidence%2F)).

issue.title: [post-training] Mochi hero SFT (step 400,407) weakness analysis: benchmark gaps, trace failures, and candidate target skills
issue.body:
## Summary

- **Motivation:** Before choosing targeted data to add to Mochi's next SFT mix, we needed a trace-backed picture of where Mochi SFT (step 400407) lags peer open-weight models—such as MRCR-65k (26.49% vs Qwen3.6 92.08%) and IFBench (26.00% strict vs Gemma-4 43.44%)—rather than extrapolating from Snowball-only defects.
- **Goal:** Identify Mochi SFT (step 400407)'s clearest benchmark and trace-level weaknesses against peer open-weight models, check mode and SFT-mix coverage gaps, and test targeted SFT data candidates for Mochi's next SFT mix.
- **Data:** 12 completed full-size benchmark runs, BFCL ×5 (issue 11538), a partial SWE-smith screen (469 retained attempts), three controlled thinking-off versus thinking-on probes, the frozen 216-store SFT manifest (968,596 packs), and two synthetic SFT datasets (multi-needle retrieval and cue-balanced tool abstention).
- **Method:** Audit error traces, run matched thinking-off versus thinking-on probes and zero-training inference checks on Mochi, scan all 216 SFT stores for thinking-off tool coverage and placeholder arguments, and evaluate a 1-hour FP32 Snowball continuation with 120 multi-needle retrieval packs (loss weight 30) against a 1-hour general-only control on full 901-item MRCR-65k.
- **Results:** Clear benchmark gaps were MRCR-65k (26.49% vs Qwen3.6 92.08%), IFBench (26.00% strict vs Gemma-4 43.44%), BFCL live-irrelevance (65.5%), and SWE-smith read calls with an extra `command` key (69/469 attempts). At a matched 4,096-token cap, Mochi scored 81.67% (98/120) under thinking-off versus 96.67% (116/120) under thinking-on on deterministic constraints, and over-called on 57/60 missing-argument tool prompts under thinking-off versus 59/59 abstention passes under thinking-on (a system-prompt guard still over-called on 35/60; empty-think prefill still emitted reasoning on 120/120). The 216-store scan found 14,718 thinking-off rows across non-coding tool stores (vs 506,889 thinking-on rows in `agentic_v1/v2` alone) and 2,485 grounding-filtered explicit placeholder calls in `agentic_v1/tool_calling` (7,383 raw across four agentic stores). On Snowball, the 1-hour multi-needle retrieval run scored 21.20% vs 21.44% control (−0.24 pp) under thinking-off and 22.65% vs 21.59% (+1.06 pp) under thinking-on on MRCR-65k, with 175/901 unclosed think spans under thinking-on.
- **Conclusion:** Multi-needle retrieval data did not transfer to headline MRCR-65k in this single 1-hour Snowball run and stays held out of Mochi's SFT mix. Thinking-off tool abstention data, placeholder-argument filtering across the agentic stores, and a matched thinking-mode check on full IFBench remain the leading candidates for Mochi's next SFT mix, while hard-math, knowledge, and major agentic benchmarks remain unmeasured on Mochi.

## 2. Trace-Backed Failure Analysis

### 2.1 `mrcr-65k` (26.49%, n=901; all 901 classified, 15 read directly)

Mochi prepends the exact requested 10-character random string on **806/901 (89.46%)** of prompts, and **186/901 (20.6%)** score `> 0.9` on MRCR's graded string-similarity metric. Mean `mrcr_accuracy` declines with needle count and across the four length buckets below 40k (`n_chars // 4`); the single 40k+ item scored 80.78%:

| Slice | n | Mean `mrcr_accuracy` |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2 needles | 299 | 36.29% |
| 4 needles | 302 | 28.71% |
| 8 needles | 300 | **14.47%** (graded string similarity) |
| 0–10k (`n_chars // 4`) | 325 | 31.68% |
| 10–20k (`n_chars // 4`) | 283 | 27.15% |
| 20–30k (`n_chars // 4`) | 159 | 20.05% |
| 30–40k (`n_chars // 4`) | 133 | 19.66% |
| 40k+ (`n_chars // 4`) | 1 | 80.78% |

Across the **620** items that hit the exact random prefix with `score <= 0.9`:
- **423 / 620 (68.2%)** matched another same-topic occurrence by a 60-character substring heuristic, with **331** matched occurrences later than the requested one and **92** earlier (measured direction; not opportunity-normalized). Under literal stripped-output equality with the same topic heuristic, **323 / 620 (52.1%)** matched another same-topic occurrence (**275** later, **48** earlier).
- **26 / 620 (4.2%)** matched a different-topic assistant turn under the 60-character substring heuristic.
- **171 / 620 (27.6%)** had no classified alternative-turn match under this heuristic (this residual count does not separate paraphrases from partial or truncated outputs).
- The remaining **95 / 901 (10.5%)** failed the exact-prefix check (`score = 0`).

`ds-1000-local` sits inside Snowball 10/05's (`27.85% [23.12–31.00]`, k=6) and Qwen3.6-35B's (`26.75% [23.50–28.50]`, k=9) observed ranges, slightly below Nemotron-3.5-30B's range (`28.46% [27.50–30.50]`, k=9), and below Gemma-4-26B (`41.50%`, k=1). Its error breakdown differs from comparators:

In the single checked comparator runs from EvalDash, timeouts were 1–6/200 (Qwen3.6: 1, Nem3.5-30B: 3, Gemma-4: 4, Snowball 10/05: 6).
- **Inspected Terminus-2 trajectories (25 total: 10 timeout-0, 10 clean-0, 2 tmux-0, 3 timeout-1):**
  - In the 10 inspected timeout failures (10–20 agent steps, ~7.4k–8.5k completion tokens), Mochi repeatedly rewrote `/workspace/solution/solution.py` (4–9 times) and ran custom import/`runpy` checks until hitting 1,800 s (one passing timeout, `ds-1000/541`, timed out right on Terminus-2's `"task_complete": true` confirmation turn).
  - In the 10 inspected exception-free failures (4–15 steps), Mochi wrote runnable code and marked the task complete while missing part of the prompt or execution contract (e.g., `ds-1000/104` replaced `&` with `&` without evaluating the resulting expression; `ds-1000/127` hardcoded `df.sample(n=1, random_state=0)` instead of sampling 20% of rows).

### 2.5 `gsm8k-0shot` (83.55% = 1,102/1,319; all 217 failures classified, 20 read) — Extractor-Sensitivity Caveat

- **145 / 217 misses (66.8%) contain the normalized gold number in the final 250 characters under the regex used here.** Of those, **29** also match a verification keyword (`check`/`verify`/`double-check`/`confirm`) and **116** do not. The other **72** did not match the gold-number heuristic.
- This flags candidates for extractor sensitivity (in inspected replies, Mochi stated the gold number and then either restated a prompt quantity or appended a verification equation whose final number the last-number regex picked up). A verified corrected accuracy was not measured, so this audit neither estimates a corrected GSM8K score nor rules out genuine arithmetic errors.

## 3. Proposed Candidate Target Skills (with Fast-Eval Proposals and Non-Eval Data Ideas)

*Data hygiene rule:* **Eval-side traces and benchmark prompts/outputs are never used as training data.** Every training data proposal below relies exclusively on freshly synthesized or non-eval open templates verified programmatically. Probe runtimes below are rough estimates and not yet measured on Mochi's serve.

### Proposal 1: Long-Context Ordinal Multi-Needle Retrieval and Verbatim Copy
- **Target gap:** Largest observed deficit vs peers (`mrcr-65k` 26.49% vs Qwen3.6 92.08% and Nemotron-3.5-30B 45.75%), with 423/620 prefix-matching low-score items matching a different same-topic occurrence by 60-character substring (323 under literal stripped-output equality), predominantly later than requested.
- **Proposed fast eval (rough estimate: minutes-scale):** A 100–200 item synthetic multi-needle probe at 8K–64K context (2/4/8 repeated-topic needles, querying the *k*-th 1-indexed occurrence with a random prefix), scored deterministically in Python by exact prefix and string similarity without an LLM judge.
- **Proposed clean training data:** Programmatically synthesize multi-turn dialogues (8K–64K tokens) mixing filler turns with 2–12 repeated requests on fresh non-MRCR topics, paired with final-turn ordinal retrieval queries distributed uniformly over *k* from 1 to *N* (covering both `/think` counting chains and `/nothink` direct-copy targets).

### Proposal 2: Strict Verifiable Constraint Following and Output Discipline
- **Target gap:** Strict instruction-following gap vs peers (`ifbench` 26.00% strict vs Gemma-4 43.44%, DeepSeek-V4-Flash 40.00%, Nemotron-3.5-120B 38.00%, Qwen3.6 34.57%), with `repeat` (0.00%), `sentence` (3.57%), `words` (11.76%), and `ratio` (15.91%) lowest.
- **Proposed fast eval (rough estimate: minutes-scale):** A 200-item held-out synthetic constraint suite covering word/sentence/ratio/repeat/format/no-preamble constraints, scored purely by deterministic Python verifiers without an LLM judge.
- **Proposed clean training data:** Programmatically compose fresh prompts combining 1–3 verifiable lexical/structural constraints (forbidden/required words, exact sentence/word counts, keyword-per-sentence, ratio bounds, strict JSON/markdown structure, no preamble/postscript), generate candidates, and **rejection-sample strictly using deterministic Python verifiers** (keeping only 100%-passing responses across both `/think` and `/nothink` formats).

### Proposal 3: Tool-Schema Adherence and Abstention Across Diverse Tool Contracts
- **Target gap:** Addresses the concrete tool-contract weaknesses observed in BFCL x5 (`simple-java` 53.3%, `parallel` 62.9%, `live-irrelevance` 65.5%) and the extra-`"command"` `read`/malformed-call defects observed in SWE-smith r6 (69/469 attempts with extra `"command"` on parsed `read`; 12/19 readout-`BAD` first-tool `read`; 21/58 exception-free `reward=0` raw `<tool_call>` text).
- **Proposed fast eval (rough estimate: minutes-scale):** A 150–200 item single-turn synthetic tool-calling probe testing: (a) unfamiliar file/code tool schemas deliberately distinct from `str_replace_editor` (checking valid Hermes JSON and zero undeclared keys), (b) irrelevance/abstention prompts requiring an explicit empty tool list or required artifact, and (c) parallel and typed-argument multi-call prompts. Graded deterministically by JSON-schema and AST checks without container spinup.
- **Proposed clean training data:** Synthesize diverse tool definitions (varying parameter names across file readers/editors, SQL/API clients, and typed Java/JS/Python signatures) with programmatically verified trajectories teaching strict adherence to declared JSON schemas, calibrated abstention when no tool applies or required arguments are missing, and parallel call arrays.

---

## 4. What Is Missing to Decide (Absence of Completed Full-Size Scores in This Snapshot)

In the retained EvalDash cache for `mochi-sft-step400407` (46 recorded runs: 23 `succeeded`, 20 `step_failed`, 2 `infra_failed`, 1 `running`), the following benchmarks have no completed full-size score. sourceStates.title: [task-curation] Decontaminate the kept population lexically
sourceStates.body:
Run lexical decontamination as a source-pipeline stage between filter and
verification. A `DecontaminationEngine` injected on `SourcePipelineConfig` — the
same pattern as `Reviewer` and `GradingMachines` — renders every kept row's
conversation with the shared renderer and marks it against one frozen eval
corpus. The stage records the measurement in the source manifest and a
`lexical/` view (`measurement.json`, per-task `task_flags`, drop manifest). A
training source rejects contaminated kept rows (`lexical:contaminated`) before
verification, so `final/` holds the retained population; evaluation and
benchmark sources keep every task and record the measurement only. Without an
engine the stage is skipped, the manifest's `lexical` section stays `null`, and
the artifact identity is unchanged.

The engine is injected rather than built in because `lib/taskcompendium` cannot
import `marin`, where the decontamination engine (`marin.datakit.decon`) lives.
`DatakitDecontamination` (experiments-side) binds it: builds or adopts the
source's document-frequency drop set, marks with the prebuilt bloom, and
attributes every match through the eval hash index into eval IDs and benchmark
families (via `hash_to_evals` in `marin.datakit.decon` and the eval-family map
in `experiments/datakit/decontam/eval_families.py`). The driver passes the
frozen corpus through `--lexical-bloom`, `--lexical-global-drop-set`,
`--lexical-corpus-version` and optional `--lexical-frozen-drop-sets`. The
engine identity enters `pipeline_identity` only when an engine is configured,
and records only the processed source's adopted drop set, so enabling the
stage or changing the corpus yields a new artifact identity without re-keying
sources that never decontaminate.

Acceptance against the sealed `ASDiv:asdiv` receipt (#12399): the
`lexical_reproduction` harness runs the FULL source pipeline on the pinned
source with the receipt's frozen bloom and drop sets, so the stage path itself
(population render, mark, attribution, training gate, export) produces the
compared evidence. It compares per-task marks over the stage's whole measured
population (read from the normalize view filtered to the task flags —
contaminated rows included), retained IDs from `final/`, and text digests
against the sealed population, flags and drop manifest
(`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/lexical-reproduction/reproduction.json`,
job `/benfeuer/lexical-reproduction-asdiv-8` on cw-us-east-02a):

- Per-task marks identical on all 2294 shared tasks — contaminated,
  max_overlap, matched_hashes, matched_eval_ids, matched_eval_families
  (0 mismatches).
- Rendered texts identical on every shared task; the shared-subset text digest
  matches the sealed population under the same chain scheme.
- Retention identical: the stage admits 410 tasks and the sealed release
  retains the same 410 IDs (the drop manifest's complement); contaminated
  rejected 1884.
- The sealed receipt measured 2305 tasks with 1895 contaminated (fraction
  0.82213, mean overlap 0.75745); the stage measured 2294 with 1884
  contaminated (0.82127, 0.75674). The 11-task delta is fully accounted for:
  10 rows main's converter now rejects at conversion (below), plus one row
  the stage's within-source dedup rejects as `exact_semantic_duplicate` of a
  row it keeps (main's audit dedups by semantic key and keeps the first row;
  the sealed census deduped by exact contract and kept both variants).

The 2,295 vs 2,305 census delta is the intended effect of two verifyit changes
made after the 2026-11-12 measurement: #11517 added conversion-time reference
validation (2026-11-15) and #11989 made math parsing reject partially parsed
expressions (2026-11-24). Before #11989, six of the ten text answers parsed
into numeric fragments ("3:30 p.m." → 3, "The 60th caller." → 60,
"11:55 p.m. on 24 December 2014." → 2014), so a reply "60" scored 1.0 against
"Who was the 60th caller?"; the other four never parsed and were emitted only
because the conversion gate did not yet exist. #11989 names this consequence
("TaskCompendium converts invalid references to `invalid_reference` instead of
grading against a fragment") and carries its own frozen-set audit. The ASDiv
converter is byte-identical on main and the branch. Not a regression; no
separate bug filed.

The sealed record's full-population `text_sha256` chains in the
measurement-time build's iteration order, which the frozen parquet does not
preserve, so full-population digest equality is not claimed; population
identity rests on per-task text equality plus the shared-subset digest.
`task_specs_sha256` pins schema-0.30 serializations; main's pipeline is
schema-0.31.

Part of #12399.

sourceStates.title: [rl] Align Arrow text widths before combining SkyRL task inputs
sourceStates.body:
read_prompt_files passed per-source datasets straight to
datasets.concatenate_datasets, which fails with "The features can't be
aligned" when the same column is string in one source and large_string in
another. The Mochi campaign run v2-mix-009 died at startup this way on
task_sha256, task_spec and runtime.

Widen compatible text columns to large_string before concatenation,
including all-narrow-string mixes so text columns carry one canonical
width, and keep rejecting incompatible non-text schemas. Mixed-width
Parquet regression tests verify that task JSON, hashes, routes and numeric
values survive concatenation. Widening covers top-level columns only;
nested text, such as the source-format prompt message lists, keeps its
original width and still raises on mixed widths.

sourceStates.title: [evals] Release eval policies with a pinned manifest and tag
sourceStates.body:
Once an eval policy is released, each of its scores should trace to one fixed run and commit. `policy release` records that.

Each policy run (one model on one evaluation) has a directory holding `record.json`, a summary of the run, and `results/`, every prompt, reply and grade. A run's ID begins with a hash of its inputs: model, evaluation settings, evaluator code, judge and vLLM build. A run is compliant if it passes `policy verify`'s checks.

Run from a clean commit on `main`, `release` picks for each baseline model and evaluation a compliant full run whose inputs hash matches this commit's, possibly from an earlier commit. It stops if any pair has none. A shared grader can change a score without changing a run's inputs, so for runs from earlier commits it prints the commits since that touched evaluation code, for the release reviewer to read. It then writes a manifest, `policy-releases/<version>.json` beside the eval records, listing each run with its commit, scores and a hash of its record and results, and tags the commit `eval-policy-<version>`. The manifest can be created only once, and a released version launches only from its tag.

A patch is a new version naming the released one as `base`: runs whose inputs changed only in the version name are reused, so fixing one evaluation reruns only it. `verify` now saves its verdict beside each record for EvalDash to read, and also requires every attempt a run selected to have finished.

Part of #10197

sourceStates.title: [evaldash] Admit released eval policy cohorts
sourceStates.body:
EvalDash groups runs into cohorts by their version label. Today an eval policy version is an unverified cohort that admits any run with its label, including smoke tests and broken runs.

This makes a released policy version (#12405) a verified cohort. It holds the runs its release manifest names, at the manifest's scores, including runs a patch reuses from its base. It also holds the version's other runs that `policy verify` found compliant and complete at the release commit, such as a checkpoint evaluated after the release. Its remaining runs are listed as rejected, with the reason. Other cohorts are unchanged.

The ingest job stores the manifests and verdict files in one new table (migration 0005, which only adds the table). EvalDash can't see git tags, so it treats every manifest as released.

Part of #10197

sourceStates.title: [evals] Add LiveCodeBench restricted to problems absent from hero training data
sourceStates.body:
676 of the 1,055 LiveCodeBench release_v6 problems have near-verbatim copies in the hero training data. This PR adds `livecodebench-hero-clean`, the same benchmark restricted to the 379 problems with no copy.

It reuses LiveCodeBench's converter, grader, dataset pin and protocol settings; only the row selection, name and population differ. The kept question IDs are in `livecodebench_hero_clean.json`. They are passed to the row selector, so editing the list changes the corpus identity. The source sets `variant="hero-clean"` because the curation driver keys sources by origin and dataset and would otherwise drop it. The existing `livecodebench` corpus identity is unchanged.

The issue has the scan method and the Qwen3-8B validation.

Fixes #12408

sourceStates.title: [rl] Overlap S3 checkpoint writes with policy training
sourceStates.body:
**Checkpoint performance.** On three Mochi runs before this change, a synchronous checkpoint save took 8.8–9.1 minutes at the median and checkpoint saves accounted for about 17% of completed-update wall time. With async staging, the two-H100 smoke handed control back to the trainer in 24.8–26.2 seconds across four saves of a 5.52 GiB checkpoint payload. That measures the staging handoff. The smoke exports at every save, and a matched Mochi run is still needed to measure the change in update wall time. [Mochi timing dashboard](https://grafana.oa.dev/d/marin-rl-runs?var-training_type=async&var-cluster=cw-us-east-08a&var-run=rl-data-campaign%2Fv3-mix-036-2026.11.26.540&var-job=%2Fbenfeuer%2Fmochi-campaign-v3-mix-036-2026.11.26.540%2Frl-data-campaign-v3-mix-036-2026.11.26.540-aa8fd6b3392d&from=1795725000000&to=1795800180000) · [H100 smoke receipt](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fpower%2Fcheckpoints%2Fskyrl-port-smoke%2Fresume%2F2026.11.27.1847%2Fterminal.json)

SkyRL pauses policy training while each rank copies its assigned checkpoint records into host memory. The ranks stream the copies to S3 in parallel. Training advances after every rank has finished copying and Megatron has written its small local control files. This removes bulk S3 writes from the update's critical path when the largest rank's share fits in the host buffer.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Complete optimizer update"] --> B["Megatron assigns checkpoint records to policy ranks"]
    B --> C["Each rank copies its records into a bounded CPU buffer"]
    C --> D["A background writer streams buffered records to S3"]
    D -->|"Release buffer space"| C
    C -->|"Each rank has copied its last record"| R["Release references to the original tensors"]
    R -->|"All ranks reached the handoff"| M["Write Megatron control files locally"]
    M --> E["Start the next optimizer update"]
```

`trainer.policy.megatron_config.checkpoint_max_staged_host_bytes` defaults to 16 GiB per rank. A rank whose share exceeds its budget waits for buffered records to drain. A single record larger than the budget uses the buffer alone.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant T as Trainer
    participant W as Policy ranks
    participant I as Inference engines
    participant S as S3
    T->>W: Stage optimizer and model state
    W-->>T: CPU staging and local control files ready
    T->>T: Register pending publication
    par Next update
        T->>I: Wake colocated inference
        T->>W: Run policy training
    and Checkpoint publication
        W->>S: Finish shards and checkpoint metadata
        W-->>T: All shard and metadata writes succeeded
        T->>S: Write trainer and rollout state
        T->>S: Publish the resume marker
        T->>T: Run on_save
    end
```

DCP write collectives run on a separate Gloo group. Later saves, exports that consume the checkpoint, and finalization wait for the pending publication. The on-disk checkpoint format stays compatible with existing readers.

The fully reshardable optimizer format gathers state on DP rank zero for each model slice before staging. Mochi's DP-reshardable format keeps optimizer shards on their owning ranks. Its restore requires the same non-DP geometry.

The port smoke pins the resume artifact after binding its training dependency.

The prompt-pool admission rule added in #12179 requires a fourth, so the [Nov 27 nightly](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/46051210355/job/140682690820) failed before comparing the two batch builders. sourceStates.title: [iris] Share pinned GPU autotune inputs across ranks
sourceStates.body:
Pin one FineStore autotune manifest at GPU job submission when the caller supplies `IRIS_AUTOTUNE_STORE_ROOT`, then pass its commit ID to every task. Local rank 0 stages that manifest into a fresh task-attempt directory on each node and publishes a ready marker after the fetch. Other local ranks wait for the same directory. A failed fetch aborts the attempt. Multi-process jobs run XLA at autotune level 0 in cache read mode and reject writable autotune overrides. Attempt directories are removed after the local processes exit.

Without a configured regional store root, workers use the `empty` snapshot and untuned kernels. A tuned root should be keyed by GPU variant, jaxlib, and CUDA runtime versions. Single-process jobs use clean attempt directories and the same compatibility key for their writable file set. The [controlled 64-H100 read-mode run](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11935#issuecomment-7063354322) found 64 identical executables and no autotune-directory writes. A dirty-host 64-GPU run of this branch, its cold-compile HLO check, and tuned step-time and power measurements remain to be done before the PR is ready for review. CPU tests check exact XLA flag values and read-only file modes; they cannot execute GPU XLA.

The focused FineStore snapshot and Iris suites passed 263 tests. An isolated Pyrefly check on changed source files reported zero errors. Repository-wide Pyrefly reports missing optional packages, including FastAPI and Polars, in this narrow local environment. The affected test runner stopped at two failures in untouched Harbor tests (S3 deadline and temporary-directory cleanup); both passed when rerun in isolation. #12229 separately changes level-0 uploader behavior; this branch's multi-process path starts no uploader.

Part of #11935

sourceStates.title: [iris] Check image build and push access before checkpoints
sourceStates.body:
Before a controller checkpoint, rollout preflight now checks the selected buildx builder, including `BUILDX_BUILDER`, for registry-cache export support. It derives image and cache repositories from the build path and verifies each GHCR push grant by starting and aborting an empty upload with Docker's credentials. Denied or inconclusive grants fail the gate with an explicit result.

The new probes use the existing `Need` dispatcher, which already maps requirements to `CheckResult`; a second probe protocol would duplicate that contract.

Focused rollout and image-build tests pass (51 tests), along with lint and Pyrefly. The broad affected-test run timed out with 405 failures across 1,597 selected tests; many Taskforge async failures came from the mixed-package pytest configuration, and a representative failure reproduces on `origin/main`. No live GHCR push probe was run locally.

sourceStates.title: [task-curation] Score AceCode candidate failures as zero

sourceStates.title: [verifyit] Grade labelled math choices by letter or value
sourceStates.body:
Accept the option letter or an equivalent value for anchored math references such as `\textbf{(D)}\ 7`. A reply that gives both must match both.

Parsing the entire reference as a product rejected standalone answers and let a wrong letter compare equal when the choice value was zero. The grader now checks the letter before comparing the value with the existing math parser.

sourceStates.title: [verifyit] Grade whole answers on unboxed math lines
sourceStates.body:
Read the final claim from the last nonempty line of an unboxed math reply. Grade the whole expression so `The answer is \frac{\pi}{4}.` earns credit against `\frac{\pi}{4}`, and `The answer is -8i.` scores zero against `-8`. Unreadable final answers score zero.

The long-loop SkyRL shell harness grades plain-text replies from `numina_math`, `deepscaler`, `hardmath@rhs`, `hendrycks_math` (algebra), `aime_1983_2024`, `dapo_math`, and `gsm8k` with VerifyIt's default `ANCHORED` profile. The whole-final-answer rule applies to unboxed `ANCHORED` submissions through TaskCompendium's in-process grader and VerifyIt's workspace-file grader. The separate MarinSkyRL `math500` task-curation variant also uses the default profile and can see verdict changes on unboxed replies. Polaris uses its own script grader. [SkyRL math conversion](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6f3981ed48432a36faaf50825cb575b1e8cc6959/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/skyrl/math.py#L238-L251) · [VerifyIt entry points](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6f3981ed48432a36faaf50825cb575b1e8cc6959/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py#L633-L656) · [Polaris grader](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d5ca98a856bffcfc6d13d079beda060b1d8cd149/experiments/post_training/long_loop/resources/polaris_grade.py#L161-L165)

For the campaign's constructed `The answer is R.` replies, 373,623 `numina_math` rows with correct replies that scored zero on main now earn credit, and 429,319 keep their verdicts. In the wrong-choice probe, all 207 `numina_math` replies that earned credit by starting with the reference's number now score zero. The correct-answer probe also found false negatives on main in `deepscaler` (8,565), `hardmath@rhs` (554), `hendrycks_math` algebra (283), and `aime_1983_2024` (1). The probed correct replies in `dapo_math` and `gsm8k` already earned credit. [Campaign probes in #12418](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/12418)

The unboxed `ANCHORED` path grades no replies in sealed Micro210, the frozen curated eval corpora, or EvalLite. Micro210 runs its pinned Evalchemy graders. The curated eval corpora use benchmark-specific scorers, and EvalLite's MATH500 and AIME24 tasks use Evalchemy's boxed scorer. Frozen-policy scores are unaffected. [Sealed Micro210 graders](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/5ca48a7ee9e8514d80cc7172776258172a5990b0/experiments/evaluation/micro210_grader/eval/graders) · [Curated math scorers](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6f3981ed48432a36faaf50825cb575b1e8cc6959/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/evalchemy/math.py#L58-L138) · [EvalLite sources](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6f3981ed48432a36faaf50825cb575b1e8cc6959/docs/references/task-curation.md#evallite)

sourceStates.title: [marin] Stop steps that lost their lease from writing results
sourceStates.body:
`run_step` now confirms that the worker still holds the step's lease before
it writes the step record, `SUCCESS`, or `FAILED`. A worker whose lease was
taken over raises `LeaseLostError` and leaves the new owner's status and
record in place. Before, the lost lease was noticed only when `step_lock`
exited, after those writes, so a late failure could mark a completed step
`FAILED` and the next launch reran it.

The check is a lease refresh, so it also restarts the 90-second staleness
window just before the write. The heartbeat and the check run on different
threads; a lock in `StatusFile.refresh_lock` keeps their conditional writes
from conflicting with each other. Rigging's `lease_refresh` retries failures
but does not report a lost lease to its caller, which `step_lock` needs, so
the heartbeat stays local.

The heartbeat also stopped on the first refresh error other than
`LeaseLostError`, including the `FileExistsError` that object-store leases
raise when a conditional write conflicts. The thread ended, the lease went
stale after 90 seconds, and another launch could take the step while this
one kept running and finished without reporting the loss. The heartbeat now
logs the error and retries at the next 30-second interval. It does not give
up: a refresh that succeeds after an outage still holds the lease, because
the lease records its holder rather than its age, and a lease taken over
during the outage fails the next refresh or write check.

This is the issue's first option, and it keeps the output layout unchanged.
Writes made by the step function itself or inside a submitted Fray job are
not checked, and a write delayed past the 90-second window after its check
can still overlap a new owner. The staging-directory design in the issue's
research comment, which publishes the winner with a conditional write, would
close those gaps.

Fixes #12407

sourceStates.title: [iris] Avoid checkpoint rollback when controller restart never begins
sourceStates.body:
Keep the previous controller rollout record when a restart fails before changing controller resources. VM restarts check SSH before GCE updates startup metadata; Kubernetes restarts check credentials and prerequisites before applying resources. The pre-deploy checkpoint remains available without arming a restore on the next boot.

Automatic rollback still runs after a forward bootstrap may have changed the database. If that rollback cannot begin, preserve the pending deploy record and its rollback coordinates so the operator can retry. An explicit rollback that cannot begin restores its prior record.

Fixes #11879

- Non-agentic release: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/benfeuer/long-loop/rl-data/smartie-mixed-20261110-v1/manifest.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fbenfeuer%2Flong-loop%2Frl-data%2Fsmartie-mixed-20261110-v1%2Fmanifest.json)). Manifest SHA-256 `94f21b06fedc6dce7184e783dab1349f1c14fed05fab3d47fcace61d2386701a`; `nonagentic-train.parquet` SHA-256 `c8948b3c13957ee054b4b8b5553127f75c44a50577b5b2b798261e9f8a5abc45`.

The bundle includes exact file URLs, identities, exclusions and overlap receipts. Seven historical upstream HF revisions remain unknown; the consumed materialized Parquet and actual evaluation tasks are independently pinned. Exact overlap checks do not establish semantic decontamination. SWE setup can resolve different dependency versions on a future run; this is not a bit-identical environment claim.

#### Micro eval policy and scores

Dataset [Marin-Micro-Eval-210 at `4564ed081c316bc3231ae5c3a53a46b39248c819`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Micro-Eval-210/tree/4564ed081c316bc3231ae5c3a53a46b39248c819); runtime wheels [Marin-Mini-Eval-Policy-Index `runtime-v4/wheels` at `d5dd315d58f0f47514dd0a2208e90e2a48541328`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Mini-Eval-Policy-Index/tree/d5dd315d58f0f47514dd0a2208e90e2a48541328/runtime-v4/wheels). Policy: 10 tasks per available benchmark, fixed per-task repetitions from the bundled eval YAML, Pi 0.87, 65,536 context, 16,384 tokens/turn, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95, judge [MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8 at `c5454eb03678d8710e54a4e0fc681b9f3b4a3dba`](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8/tree/c5454eb03678d8710e54a4e0fc681b9f3b4a3dba). Tau3 was excluded: 200 distinct tasks across 20 benchmarks, expanded to 440 pinned attempt slots.

The final result is 439 scored + one explicitly unscored DNA assembly slot (UID399). Recovery restarted only eight slots whose task startup failed from unnecessary judge-relay injection, using the same task/repetition identities, best-16 model, eval seed and sampling settings; it yielded seven grades. Model-side errors stayed scored; all 432 original scored rows were preserved. Mean scored-attempt reward is 0.4525643127; the unweighted mean of 20 benchmark means is 0.5216066358. Before recovery: 432 scored / eight unscored, with means 0.4529530863 / 0.5186440986. These are heterogeneous partial-credit reward means; they are not pass@1. No paired baseline establishes an RL improvement.

#### Evidence and limits

- Final scores and attempt lineage: `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/users/benfeuer/long-loop/long-loop/report/2026.11.12.12/evaluation.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fbenfeuer%2Flong-loop%2Flong-loop%2Freport%2F2026.11.12.12%2Fevaluation.json)), SHA-256 `6a110a2615f40c5a89eee763f7b021a4b66499760abd7bdd7db2b2a6a4865d3a`.
